fin-b1-explain-variance-narrative.q: You paste a budget variance table but only gave context for 2 of the 15 line items. What should the prompt force the AI to do for the other 13?
options: Invent a plausible driver so the report reads as complete
Write "driver not provided — confirm with [owner]" instead of guessing a cause
Recalculate the variance using its own estimate of typical business drivers
Skip those line items entirely without any note
fin-b1-explain-variance-narrative.why: The "driver not provided" instruction is the core anti-hallucination guardrail — it stops the model from inventing a plausible-sounding cause for a variance you never explained.

fin-b1-explain-variance-narrative.q: A variance table has 15 line items but only 2 are actually significant. Why set a materiality threshold before drafting the narrative?
options: So the narrative focuses only on variances above a meaningful dollar or percent amount, instead of treating a $200 rounding gap the same as a $50,000 miss
So every line item gets equal word count in the summary
So the AI can skip verifying any numbers
So the report only needs one sentence total
fin-b1-explain-variance-narrative.why: Without a materiality threshold, the narrative buries the two variances that actually matter under a dozen trivial ones.

fin-b1-explain-variance-narrative.q: Before sending an AI-drafted variance narrative to management, what should the analyst do?
options: Nothing — the numbers were pasted verbatim so they must be correct
Independently recompute at least two of the variance percentages against the source table
Ask the AI to double-check its own math one more time
Only check that the tone sounds professional
fin-b1-explain-variance-narrative.why: Independently recomputing a couple of figures catches transcription or computation errors before the narrative reaches anyone else.

fin-b2-summarize-filings-for-briefing.q: Why require the AI to note which section (e.g., "MD&A", "Q3 highlights") each cited number came from?
options: It's required by SEC formatting rules
It turns verification into a quick lookup instead of a full re-read of the whole filing
It lets the AI recalculate the number more accurately
It makes the summary sound more authoritative
fin-b2-summarize-filings-for-briefing.why: Naming the source section is what makes checking every number fast and practical under time pressure before a briefing.

fin-b2-summarize-filings-for-briefing.q: An excerpt says revenue was "up 6% year over year, driven primarily by higher unit volumes." How should the summary treat the stated driver versus an AI-added explanation for the guidance raise?
options: Treat both as equally reliable since they came from the same document
Quote the stated driver directly, and label anything the AI infers (like an unstated cause for the guidance raise) as "inference, not stated directly"
Omit both since neither can be fully trusted
Rewrite the driver in the analyst's own words for clarity
fin-b2-summarize-filings-for-briefing.why: Separating what's explicitly stated from what's inferred prevents a briefing from including an unlabeled inference as if it were a quoted management fact.

fin-b2-summarize-filings-for-briefing.q: Which of these is the biggest confidentiality risk when using this workflow?
options: Pasting content from a paid, licensed research terminal or non-public data into a general AI tool
Using bullet points instead of paragraphs
Summarizing a public 10-K excerpt
Structuring the output into five labeled sections
fin-b2-summarize-filings-for-briefing.why: Public filings are generally safe to paste, but paid vendor research or non-public data usually is not and should be checked against firm policy first.

fin-i1-analysis-framework-checklist.q: Why should you build this checklist as a fully generic template with no real company or deal data?
options: It's faster to type
It's itself a confidentiality guardrail — the checklist-building conversation never needs to touch sensitive information at all
The AI performs worse with specific data
Generic templates are required by SEC rules
fin-i1-analysis-framework-checklist.why: Keeping the request generic means no real company or deal data ever has to enter the AI tool while you build the reusable framework.

fin-i1-analysis-framework-checklist.q: Why ask the AI to mark each checklist item as needing verified external data versus data you can reason from your own figures?
options: To make the checklist look longer
It builds a verification checkpoint directly into the structure of the framework itself
It's a formatting requirement for compliance software
It tells you which items to skip entirely
fin-i1-analysis-framework-checklist.why: Separating verified-data items from reasoned items embeds a checkpoint into the framework instead of leaving verification as an afterthought.

fin-i1-analysis-framework-checklist.q: What's wrong with asking the AI to build this checklist using details from a real, current deal you're working on?
options: It makes the checklist more accurate
It turns a reusable template request into a one-off analysis of sensitive data
The AI will produce a shorter checklist
It's slower than using generic examples
fin-i1-analysis-framework-checklist.why: Using real deal details defeats the purpose of a reusable, generic template and unnecessarily exposes sensitive information.

fin-i2-sector-research-cited-sources.q: You ask Gemini Deep Research "Tell me about the semiconductor industry." Why is this the wrong way to use it for research?
options: Gemini doesn't support broad questions
It's too broad and returns a generic synthesized narrative instead of scoped, checkable sources
It should be asked in Claude instead
It will return only outdated sources
fin-i2-sector-research-cited-sources.why: A specific question with sector, geography, and timeframe triggers retrieval of specific, checkable sources rather than a generic narrative.

fin-i2-sector-research-cited-sources.q: Why explicitly instruct Gemini Deep Research to show disagreements between sources rather than resolve them into one answer?
options: It's more interesting to read
A confidently unified answer can hide a genuine split between analysts or data providers you need to know about before citing it
Gemini is technically incapable of resolving disagreements
It reduces the number of citations shown
fin-i2-sector-research-cited-sources.why: Silently resolving disagreement into a single confident answer can hide exactly the kind of split you need to know about before using a claim.

fin-i2-sector-research-cited-sources.q: Before using a citation from a Gemini Deep Research report in a research brief, what must you do?
options: Trust the synthesized answer as the source itself
Click through and confirm the source actually supports what's claimed
Only check the publish date
Nothing — citations from Deep Research are pre-verified
fin-i2-sector-research-cited-sources.why: Deep Research's synthesized answer is a pointer to the real source, not the source itself, so every citation you plan to use should be opened and confirmed.

fin-i3-investment-memo-drafting.q: A memo section would normally need a competitor market-share figure, but it isn't in your verified notes. What should the AI do?
options: Estimate a reasonable industry figure
Insert a [VERIFY] placeholder instead of estimating
Leave that part of the section blank with no note
Omit the entire section silently
fin-i3-investment-memo-drafting.why: The [VERIFY] placeholder makes every unverified figure visibly incomplete instead of letting the model fill the gap with a plausible-sounding estimate.

fin-i3-investment-memo-drafting.q: Why does the prompt require a dedicated "key risks and what would change my mind" section?
options: It's required by regulators
It counters confirmation bias by arguing against your own thesis using only the risks you've noted
It pads out the memo's length
It replaces the need for a firm's sign-off process
fin-i3-investment-memo-drafting.why: Drafting from notes you already believe support your conclusion is a real confirmation-bias risk that this section is designed to catch.

fin-i3-investment-memo-drafting.q: What kind of data should you paste into this prompt?
options: Raw, unredacted deal or client data for maximum accuracy
Your own already-verified figures and analysis notes, not raw deal data
A competitor's non-public research note
Whatever data is fastest to copy
fin-i3-investment-memo-drafting.why: Drafting from your own pre-verified, summarized notes keeps sensitive information out of the AI tool while still getting AI-assisted structuring speed.

fin-a1-monthly-reporting-workflow.q: When mapping your monthly reporting process, which steps must the SOP mark as "must stay manual"?
options: Drafting narratives and first-pass summaries
Source data extraction, figure verification, and final sign-off
Checklist review
Formatting the narrative into board deck language
fin-a1-monthly-reporting-workflow.why: Keeping AI out of source data extraction, verification, and sign-off protects both accuracy and confidentiality at the stages where a mistake matters most.

fin-a1-monthly-reporting-workflow.q: Why does each verification checkpoint in the SOP need a named owner?
options: It's needed for payroll tracking
So checks don't get quietly skipped when the close calendar gets tight
It's a legal filing requirement
So credit can be assigned after an error
fin-a1-monthly-reporting-workflow.why: Without a named owner, verification steps are the first thing to slip under deadline pressure during a busy close.

fin-a1-monthly-reporting-workflow.q: You write the SOP but never run it end-to-end on a real reporting cycle before finalizing it. What's the risk?
options: None — a well-written SOP works the same either way
It looks good on paper but doesn't match reality under deadline pressure
The AI-generated SOP will be legally invalid
It becomes impossible to revise later
fin-a1-monthly-reporting-workflow.why: Testing the workflow against one real cycle is what surfaces gaps between the documented process and what actually happens under deadline pressure.

ins-b1-explain-policy-plain-language.q: The AI's plain-language draft mentions coverage prominently but buries the exclusions in one brief line at the end. What should you do?
options: Accept it — exclusions are secondary to coverage
Rewrite it so exclusions are given equal prominence to coverage, not buried or softened
Delete the exclusions section entirely to keep it simple
Ask the AI to make the explanation shorter overall
ins-b1-explain-policy-plain-language.why: A plain-language rewrite that softens an exclusion is exactly the kind of error that leads a client to believe they're covered when they're not.

ins-b1-explain-policy-plain-language.q: Why should the AI flag ambiguous policy wording instead of picking one interpretation?
options: Flagging takes less effort than resolving it
A confidently wrong interpretation of unclear wording is worse than an honest "this could be read two ways"
Clients prefer ambiguous answers
All state insurance regulators require it
ins-b1-explain-policy-plain-language.why: Resolving genuine ambiguity on the client's behalf risks giving them a false sense of certainty about coverage that isn't actually clear.

ins-b1-explain-policy-plain-language.q: What should never happen with the AI's plain-language policy explanation?
options: Using it as your talking-points draft for a client conversation
Sending it directly to a client as a substitute for the actual policy document
Reading it against the source wording before use
Flagging anticipated client questions from it
ins-b1-explain-policy-plain-language.why: The explanation is a talking-points draft; the actual policy document governs and must remain what the client relies on.

ins-b2-client-followups-renewal-reminder.q: Why does the prompt require exactly one call-to-action per message?
options: Shorter messages are always preferred by clients
Messages asking for two or three different things tend to get partial or no responses
Email platforms limit the number of links allowed
It reduces the message's character count for SMS delivery
ins-b2-client-followups-renewal-reminder.why: A single, clear next step is what actually gets a response, compared to a message asking the client to do several things at once.

ins-b2-client-followups-renewal-reminder.q: You don't yet know the exact premium change for a renewing client. What should the drafted message do?
options: Estimate the increase based on typical past renewals
Use only the facts explicitly provided, never inventing or approximating a figure not given
Omit the premium topic with no mention at all
Guess a round number as a placeholder
ins-b2-client-followups-renewal-reminder.why: Forcing every date and dollar figure to come verbatim from what you supplied is the anti-hallucination guardrail — a wrong premium figure has real downstream consequences.

ins-b2-client-followups-renewal-reminder.q: Which of these is a real risk this lesson warns against?
options: Requesting 2-3 tone variants to match the client relationship
Sending a message with more than one call-to-action, which lowers response rates
Using [CLIENT NAME] as a placeholder when the name wasn't given
Checking the renewal date against the system of record before sending
ins-b2-client-followups-renewal-reminder.why: Piling multiple asks into one message is a common mistake that measurably reduces how often clients respond.

ins-i1-compare-two-policy-documents.q: Two clauses in the current policy and the renewal offer are worded differently but seem to describe similar coverage. What should the comparison table do?
options: Mark them as equivalent since the wording sounds similar
Write "cannot confirm from wording — needs manual review" rather than guessing they're equivalent
Pick whichever interpretation is more favorable to the client
Leave that row blank
ins-i1-compare-two-policy-documents.why: This instruction is the key guardrail against false reassurance — it stops the model from declaring two differently-worded clauses equivalent when it can't actually be sure.

ins-i1-compare-two-policy-documents.q: Why require the AI to flag gaps in both directions — present in Document A but not B, and vice versa?
options: It makes the table look symmetrical
It catches coverage quietly dropped in a renewal, which is the change most likely to matter and go unnoticed
It's a required CRM formatting rule
It reduces the total number of table rows
ins-i1-compare-two-policy-documents.why: Bidirectional gap-flagging catches a dropped endorsement or coverage in a renewal offer, which is exactly what a client needs to know before signing.

ins-i1-compare-two-policy-documents.q: Which rows in the comparison table are the highest priority to manually verify?
options: Rows where coverage appears identical in both documents
Rows flagged as differences, especially anything marked "missing in the other document"
Only the deductible rows
Only the rows with the shortest text
ins-i1-compare-two-policy-documents.why: Flagged differences are the highest-stakes items because a missed or misstated flag directly translates into an errors-and-omissions risk.

ins-i2-claims-communication.q: A claim is partially denied due to a gradual-leak exclusion. How should the message be structured?
options: State the denial reason immediately with no acknowledgment of the client's situation
Lead with genuine acknowledgment of the client's situation, then state the confirmed facts plainly, then give next steps
Apologize extensively for the exclusion existing in the policy
Avoid stating the actual denial reason to reduce liability
ins-i2-claims-communication.why: A stressed client who feels dismissed stops absorbing information, so acknowledgment before facts is what makes the message actually land.

ins-i2-claims-communication.q: Why must denial language avoid anything that could read as admitting fault or promising coverage beyond what's confirmed?
options: It's purely a style preference
Claims communication often becomes part of a dispute record, so overstated language can create real liability
It makes the message shorter
Clients rarely reread denial explanations
ins-i2-claims-communication.why: Because claims messages can end up as part of a dispute record, language that reads as an admission or an unconfirmed promise creates real legal exposure.

ins-i2-claims-communication.q: What's a common mistake to avoid when drafting claims communication?
options: Verifying every fact against the claims system before sending
Letting the AI infer or soften the denial reason instead of stating the confirmed, actual reason
Leading with acknowledgment before facts
Offering a direct way for the client to reach you with questions
ins-i2-claims-communication.why: Softening or inferring a denial reason instead of stating the confirmed one is a factual error in an already sensitive situation.

ins-i3-objection-handling-needs-analysis.q: You're preparing needs-analysis questions for a first-time homeowner. Should the questions lead toward a specific product you want to sell?
options: Yes, leading questions get to a sale faster
No — open-ended, non-leading questions surface the client's actual coverage gaps rather than confirming a product you already had in mind
It doesn't matter as long as the facts stated are accurate
Leading questions are required for compliance documentation
ins-i3-objection-handling-needs-analysis.why: Leading questions produce answers that confirm a predetermined product, not the client's actual needs, defeating the purpose of a needs analysis.

ins-i3-objection-handling-needs-analysis.q: Why does the prompt ask the AI to flag anything in its own response that could be read as overpromising?
options: It's a compliance and trust guardrail that catches drift toward overstating coverage or pressure tactics before you use it
It makes the response shorter
It's optional and rarely changes anything
It replaces the need for any human review of the content
ins-i3-objection-handling-needs-analysis.why: Self-flagging pushes the model to catch itself if a response angle drifts toward overstating coverage, rather than leaving that entirely to your review.

ins-i3-objection-handling-needs-analysis.q: What should an agent avoid doing with AI-prepared objection responses?
options: Practicing them in their own words before the conversation
Reading them verbatim to a client instead of internalizing and personalizing them
Grounding them in real product facts
Refining them after the real conversation based on what worked
ins-i3-objection-handling-needs-analysis.why: Reading a script verbatim makes the conversation sound unnatural and means the agent doesn't truly own what they say if the client asks an unrehearsed follow-up.

ins-a1-client-communication-template-lib.q: Why organize your existing good drafts into an indexed library rather than just keeping them scattered?
options: It looks more professional to clients
It solves the real failure mode of having good drafts you can't find fast enough under time pressure
Indexing is required by most CRM software
It reduces the total number of templates you need
ins-a1-client-communication-template-lib.why: Without a searchable index, an agent under deadline pressure ends up writing from scratch anyway, defeating the purpose of the library.

ins-a1-client-communication-template-lib.q: Why should every template entry in the library include a stated verification checkpoint?
options: Templates look incomplete without one
It keeps the accuracy and confidentiality discipline intact as the library scales past a handful of messages
It's a marketing requirement for insurance websites
It removes the need to ever review a new draft
ins-a1-client-communication-template-lib.why: Baking the checkpoint into every entry preserves the same discipline from the earlier one-off prompts as the library grows.

ins-a1-client-communication-template-lib.q: What happens if you let the AI invent template types you didn't actually describe when building this library?
options: It saves time building the library
It bloats the library with template types you'll never actually use
It automatically improves accuracy
It better matches insurance industry standards
ins-a1-client-communication-template-lib.why: The prompt explicitly restricts the AI to organizing and completing what you gave it, keeping the library scoped to situations you actually handle.
